definition: Accumulated Cyclone Energy — a measure of the total wind-energy output of a tropical cyclone. Calculated as the sum of (wind speed²/10⁴) over all 6-hourly observations where wind ≥ 34 kt. Typical Atlantic season produces ~100 ACE units; a single major hurricane alone generates ~10-30 units.

A sudden and dramatic increase in a hurricane's strength. The National Hurricane Center defines RI as a wind speed increase of at least 30 kt in a 24-hour period. RI events are notoriously difficult to forecast and often lead to the most severe impacts.

A classification system based on a tropical cyclone's maximum sustained wind speed. Tropical storms are 34-63 kt; hurricanes are Category 1 (64-82 kt), Category 2 (83-95 kt), Category 3 (96-112 kt), Category 4 (113-136 kt), and Category 5 (137+ kt). The scale describes wind hazard only; storm surge, rainfall, tornadoes, and forward speed are separate risks.
The point at which the center of a tropical cyclone crosses the coast. Officially defined as the center's passage over the coastline; does not require the eye to reach land.

The speed at which a hurricane moves across the surface. Slower-moving storms can produce excessive rainfall and flooding; faster-moving storms minimize exposure duration but can still be extremely destructive.
Explosive Deepening — when central pressure drops rapidly, typically ≥20 mb in 24 hours. Indicates very rapid intensification and often precedes the strongest winds.

The Hurricane Databases maintained by NOAA's National Hurricane Center. HURDAT2 contains 6-hourly position, wind, and pressure estimates for all known tropical cyclones in the Atlantic basin dating back to 1851.

A numerical rating (1-5) for hurricanes based on sustained wind speed according to the Saffir-Simpson Scale. Higher categories indicate stronger winds, but other factors like storm surge, rainfall, and forward speed also determine overall impact.

The geographic extent of different wind-speed thresholds around a hurricane's center. Describes where 34 kt, 50 kt, and 64 kt winds are expected, helping forecast who will experience dangerous conditions.
The path of the center of a hurricane across the Earth's surface. HurricaneMap displays historical tracks as lines on the map; track position is measured every 6 hours in HURDAT2.
The U.S. state(s) where a hurricane made landfall. A single hurricane can make multiple landfalls in different states during its lifetime.
The maximum sustained wind speed recorded during a hurricane's entire lifetime. Occurs at different times for different storms and may happen over water or at landfall.
The lowest central pressure recorded during a hurricane's lifetime. Lower pressure generally corresponds to stronger winds and more intense storms. Related to wind speed but not perfectly correlated.

An abnormal rise in sea level accompanying a hurricane, primarily due to the hurricane's winds pushing water toward the coast. Can reach 20+ feet and is often the most destructive aspect of a hurricane.
A fatality (death) caused by a hurricane or its impacts. Includes direct deaths (e.g., from storm surge) and indirect deaths (e.g., from evacuation accidents or post-disaster complications).
Economic loss caused by a hurricane, typically measured in US dollars. Includes property damage, infrastructure destruction, agricultural losses, and business interruption.

Historical damage figures converted to a fixed year's dollars (e.g., 2024 USD) to account for changes in property values and construction costs. Allows fair comparison of storms across different eras.
A tropical cyclone with maximum sustained winds below 34 kt. The first stage of tropical cyclone development; can strengthen into a tropical storm or hurricane.
A tropical cyclone with maximum sustained winds between 34 and 63 kt. Named systems that have become organized enough to receive an official name from the National Hurricane Center.
A hurricane of Category 3 or higher on the Saffir-Simpson Scale, with maximum sustained winds of at least 96 kt (111 mph). This wind classification alone does not determine the storm's total impacts.
